narration.text: We give the model three tools, each with a name, a short description and a JSON schema for its inputs.
When the model wants shipping data, it calls the carrier's API directly and reads the reply.
Our code runs each requested call and sends the output back as a tool result with the matching id.
With strict mode on, the tool arguments always match our schema.
Because the arguments match the schema, we pass the customer number straight to the database with no further checks.
A tool's description is just a label for us; its wording doesn't change which tool the model picks.
If the carrier's API fails, we return the error text flagged as an error, so the model can adjust.
The model only sees our tool definitions and the results we return, never the code behind them.

planted.misconception: The model calls external APIs itself.
planted.whyWrong: The model only emits a structured tool request: a tool name and arguments. Your application runs the call (or the provider does, for its own server tools) and sends the result back. That execution step is where you enforce permissions, timeouts and logging.
acceptableCorrections: The model only requests the call; our code executes it and returns the result.
Our application executes the tool request and sends back the output.
planted.exceptions: Server tools such as a provider-hosted web search are executed by the provider, not by the model either. A carrier API you integrate is a client tool, so your application runs it.

planted.misconception: Schema-valid tool arguments are safe and correct.
planted.whyWrong: Strict mode guarantees the arguments have the right shape and types, not that the values are right or allowed. The model can pick the wrong customer, invent a value, or be steered by injected text. Your code must check the value against the logged-in user and business rules before it touches the database.
acceptableCorrections: A valid shape doesn't mean the right customer; we check it belongs to the logged-in user first.
Validate the value and the user's permission in code before calling the database.

planted.misconception: Tool descriptions don't affect which tool the model chooses.
planted.whyWrong: The model chooses tools from their names, descriptions and schemas; that text is part of the prompt. Vague or overlapping descriptions cause wrong or missed tool calls, so descriptions are written and tested like prompts, with examples and clear boundaries between similar tools.
acceptableCorrections: The description is part of the prompt, so vague wording leads to wrong tool choices; we write and test it carefully.
Clear descriptions with examples help the model choose correctly.
